Iran has asked Moscow to supply its newest Russian-developed Geran attack drones for use against Israel and the United States, according to the Financial Times, citing Western security officials and a person close to the Kremlin. It remains unclear whether Russia has agreed to the latest request. 
Iran originally supplied Russia with the Shahed technology. Russia then spent four years combat-testing, modifying and mass-producing the platform in Ukraine and Tehran now reportedly wants Russia’s evolved versions back.
The latest jet-powered Geran variants are faster, carry larger warheads and incorporate improved targeting, communications and resistance to electronic warfare. Russia’s adaptation of the Iranian design has become so extensive that CSIS recently concluded that Russia has effectively mastered the platform through continuous battlefield-driven development.

Houthis Sign Satellite Data Deals to Tighten Grip on Bab al-Mandab, Sources Say
The Houthis’ external intelligence apparatus has signed new agreements with a Chinese company to obtain satellite imagery and maritime surveillance data, intelligence sources told Sheba Intelligence.
The reported arrangements are aimed at expanding Houthi monitoring of commercial and military shipping across the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandab, Gulf of Aden and Arabian Sea, with particular focus on Saudi and allied warships.
According to the sources, the data could support missile and drone operations by providing geographic coordinates, vessel movement and speed information. The agreements were reportedly brokered through Iran’s military attaché’s office in China, linking the Chinese company with Houthi liaison officers in Muscat.
The company was identified as Meentropy Technology (Hangzhou), operating as MizarVision. US Treasury records show the company was added to the sanctions list in May 2026 under Iran-related measures.
The agreements reportedly came after the Houthis expanded control along Yemen’s Red Sea coast to Dhubab and Mayun Island, increasing their ability to combine territorial control with satellite-based maritime surveillance around one of the world’s most strategic shipping chokepoints.
Sheba Intelligence could not independently verify whether the reported agreements are operational or confirm all details of the communications and targeting arrangements.
Full report available via the link in the comments
https://shebaintelligence.uk/houthis-sign-satellite-data-deals-to-tighten-grip-on-bab-al-mandab

🤖 Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Sam Altman [Call](https://www.forbes.com/sites/gabrielalinzainescu/2026/09/13/anthropic-ceo-dario-amodei-calls-for-a-slowdown-in-frontier-ai/) For A Slowdown In Frontier AI
Dario Amodei has spent five years arguing that Anthropic could build frontier AI carefully and still win commercially. On Saturday he added a condition to that thesis: the whole industry has to ease off the accelerator.
In a roughly 3,900-word essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” the Anthropic co-founder and CEO wrote that “we must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” He was explicit that pacing does not mean halting training or technical progress. It means building in enough time for alignment work, third-party verification and operational rigor to keep up with what the models can do.
Within hours, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman posted on X that “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” adding that OpenAI would match Anthropic’s first commitment. Elon Musk’s reaction ran three words: “Dario is right.”
Amodei has been skeptical of slowdown calls before. In the essay he dismisses the 2023 “pause” letter as premature, because the models of that era could not act as coherent agents and there was little to study. He says two developments since the summer convinced him that the calculus has flipped.
📝: The only reason all the big AI CEOs are calling for a "slow down" in AI development are[ physical constraints](https://t.me/CIG_telegram/74215) in data center [construction](https://t.me/CIG_telegram/72989) and the maintenance of LLMs which need an ever increasing number of MWh to keep operating.
While they may cite cybersecurity as a reason, that hasn't stopped the development of LLMs until building data centers became impossible due to the price of raw materials (lack thereof) or opposition from the communities which were going to have to share local resources with the data centers.
Dario Amodei and Sam Altman's calls for the slow down of AI development "coincide" with China [restricting](https://t.me/CIG_telegram/83316) the export of rare earth metals necessary in data center construction, [memory chip shortages](https://t.me/CIG_telegram/76714), and a lack of energy production.
Already 5% of the U.S' energy output [is used to power](https://ourworldindata.org/data-insights/around-5-of-electricity-in-the-united-states-is-used-for-data-centers-far-more-than-the-global-average) existing data centers. The data center construction frenzy [may lead to as much as 25% the U.S' energy production](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-21/data-centers-on-track-to-suck-up-a-fifth-of-us-power-use-by-2035) being used to power data centers LLMs rely on. 
With the price of diesel skyrocketing and the looming threat of shortages of other petrochemical products which are used in the construction of data centers and computer chips, the resources to maintain the AI boom just aren't available anymore so the AI companies need an excuse to scale back and the excuse they've decided on is the "AI doomsday" shtick to show how "responsible" Amodei and Altman are with their toys.
🔗 https://www.forbes.com/sites/gabrielalinzainescu/2026/09/13/anthropic-ceo-dario-amodei-calls-for-a-slowdown-in-frontier-ai/

🤚🇮🇷Is the time ripe for Gulf kingdoms to break free from US 'kill switch' – and can Iran help?
Gulf states may reportedly seek to reduce their dependence on US arms purchases over fears of an implicit “kill switch” that gives Washington leverage over their national security.
👉 The original "kill switch" discussion stems from rumors surrounding the F-35 stealth fighter jet program and suggesting that the US could remotely render its sophisticated aircraft, as well as other top-notch weapons, ineffective. Last year, the Pentagon denied the[ claims in relation to the F-35.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/63338)
But there are indirect ways for the US to turn its customers’ arsenals into expensive and useless piles of hardware, The Cradle points out.
🔴 The US seeks to provide not just stand-alone weapons, but entire “packages” of interconnected systems
🔴 Software updates, spare parts, maintenance, and other critical support also typically come from the US
🔴 The US withholds core software and source code from its customers, keeping long-term modernization, fault diagnosis, mission-data support, and the broader sustainment chain under its control
That effectively means Gulf states have to rely on the US for major military operations and defense initiatives. While this dependence de facto constrains their sovereignty, the war with Iran exposed major gaps in the US security umbrella and the limits of Washington’s ability to[ provide effective defense support.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74268)
Hedging against the US, but still dependent
The SIPRI 2026 report shows that Gulf states remain strongly dependent on the US especially when it comes to aircraft, missiles and interceptors purchases.
Three of the world’s top 10 arms importers in 2021-25 were in the Middle East:
♦️ Saudi Arabia (6.8% of global imports)
♦️ Qatar (6.4%)
♦️ Kuwait (2.8%)
🌏 54% of arms imports to the Middle East came from the US
🌏 12% came from Italy
🌏 11% from France
🌏 7.3% from Germany
However, Gulf states increasingly recognize that relying on the US “is no longer sufficient to protect them,” given Washington’s shifting geopolitical priorities and “the growing limitations on its once-boundless military strength,” argues Khalid Al-Jaber, a scholar of Arab and Gulf studies.
👉 Al-Jaber notes that the UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and others have been gradually diversifying their military imports, with some pursuing defense cooperation with Turkey and Pakistan. These efforts signal a clear attempt to build strategic depth beyond the traditional US-led system.
Defense and new security architecture
Nobody says it out loud, but buying US weapons also means buying into [Washington’s risky military adventures. ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74503)The US-Israeli aggression against Iran has come at a heavy economic cost for the Gulf kingdoms, which were turned into American launchpads and strategic tools in the war. Qatar, Kuwait, and Bahrain have found themselves particularly exposed.
Meanwhile, Iran is proposing an entirely different approach: getting rid of US bases in the region, breaking free from Washington’s “kill switch” and its imposed wars, and building a regional security and military framework together with Iran, Iraq and the Gulf kingdoms. Apparently, these concerns will be on the agenda at a September 14 meeting in Muscat, announced by [Tehran on Friday.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74487)

🇷🇺🚀 Russia outpaces Ukraine and NATO in smart, cheap weapons — reports
Russia is fielding a new generation of relatively inexpensive, advanced weapons faster than Ukraine or the US-led West can match, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The paper points to the Geran-5 and Banderol as examples of Russia’s ability to move rapidly from design and battlefield testing to mass production. Both are estimated at around $100,000 each — a fraction of the cost of weapons such as the US Tomahawk, which runs above $2 million.
Russian engineers have steadily increased speed, range, survivability and resistance to jamming, while Western forces are still burning expensive interceptors and scrambling to build cheaper defenses.
💬 “Here in the West, we tend to underestimate Russia, but they can go very fast from idea and experimentation to production,” said Kateryna Bondar, a senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies’ Wadhwani AI Center in Washington.
The verdict from the WSJ is blunt: Russia has stolen a march on its adversaries.
Ukraine lacks the production depth for sustained competition, while the US and NATO are struggling to expand output of key systems such as Patriot interceptors and to turn new concepts into mass-produced weapons quickly enough.
And the problem for the West is only getting worse: Russia is combining scale, low cost and rapid innovation — precisely the kind of warfare NATO spent decades neglecting while chasing ultra-expensive “exquisite” systems.

🔥🇸🇦 Houthis wreak havoc on Saudi oil artery
Saudi Arabia’s strategic East–West oil pipeline was shut down as a precaution after multiple drone strikes hit facilities in the Riyadh and Medina regions, according to the Saudi Energy Ministry.
Satellite imagery shows major fire and structural damage at pumping stations near Al-Masbah and Al-Dhahrah, with smoke and heat signatures detected along the pipeline corridor.
The 1,200-km Petroline can move around 7 million barrels per day from Abqaiq to the Red Sea port of Yanbu — a crucial alternative route while shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains restricted.
Saudi authorities say the attacks caused injuries and material damage. Riyadh’s preliminary assessment says the drones came from Iraq, while Iraqi authorities said they were launched from Maysan province.
